title: Why Claude Thinks in XML (And Why Markdown Is Costing You Security & Sanity)
lead: I know what half of you are thinking: 'XML? Seriously? What is this, SOAP and Enterprise Java from 2004?!' Hear me out before you close the tab. Anthropic didn’t resurrect XML out of nostalgia. They did it because your markdown prompts are a security catastrophe waiting to happen.

items: The $1 Chevy Tahoe: In late 2023, a customer used a prompt injection on Chevrolet of Watsonville's customer chatbot, forcing it to agree to a legally binding offer to sell a brand-new 2024 Chevy Tahoe for $1.00.

The DPD Brand Meltdown: In January 2024, parcel firm DPD had to abruptly shut down its AI support system within 24 hours after users easily coaxed it into swearing, writing limericks criticizing the company, and revealing system prompts.

mentalModel.title: 1. The 60-Second Mental Model: SQL Injection vs. Prompt Injection
mentalModel.text:
Remember junior year when you learned why string-concatenating SQL queries is a crime?

SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'admin' OR '1'='1';

When you use plain markdown (# Heading or **bold**), the LLM views the entire prompt as one long stream of semantic tokens. To a neural network, there is zero fundamental difference between your instructions and the user’s text.

YES, Claude was pre-trained and fine-tuned on XML! Anthropic trained Claude using XML tags as explicit structural syntax boundaries. To Claude, an XML tag isn't just text—it is an immutable AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) container. What is inside a tag stays inside that tag.

title: Stop Rushing Your Model: Extended Thinking & The 'Whiteboard' Pattern
lead: Why do LLMs fail on edge cases in LeetCode-Hard problems or distributed concurrency checks? Because standard LLMs are forced to predict Token #1 within 50 milliseconds of reading your prompt. Let's fix that.

A failed first-turn answer that leads to 4 frustrated follow-up chat turns wastes 5.4x more total tokens than investing in 2,000 reasoning tokens on Turn #1.

mentalModel.text:
Imagine you're interviewing a Principal Engineer. You ask them to design a fault-tolerant Paxos consensus algorithm. If they blurt out C++ code within 1.5 seconds without pausing, you’d be terrified. You want them to grab a marker, sketch out split-brain edge cases on the whiteboard, scratch out a flawed idea, and only then start writing code.

Standard LLMs don’t have a whiteboard. They write the first word of code immediately, get painted into a logical corner, and hallucinate to save face. Extended Thinking gives Claude a private, invisible whiteboard.

title: Building Self-Healing Agent Loops: What Happens When Tools Crash?
lead: Building a demo agent with tool calling is easy. Building one that survives DB timeouts, schema changes, and network blips without entering a catastrophic infinite apology loop is where software engineering actually begins.

stats.title: The Failure Modes of Fragile Agents:
items: The Infinite Apology Spiral: 42% of unmanaged tool loops fail by repeatedly apologizing ('I\'m sorry, let me fix that...') until hitting the maximum token limit or API quota.
Silent Failure Cascade: Swallowing tool errors and returning empty JSON causes Claude to hallucinate mock data and pretend the operation succeeded.

mentalModel.title: 1. The 60-Second Mental Model: Circuit Breakers & Dead-Letter Queues
mentalModel.text:
In microservice architecture, when downstream Service B throws a 503, Service A doesn't immediately crash or hammer Service B in an infinite tight loop. You implement backoff and circuit breakers.

When Claude calls a tool and your backend throws a SQL syntax error, do not crash the process. Feed the error back to Claude with is_error: true. Claude treats this as an active debug signal, inspects its mistake, and rewrites the query.

topic: Loop Engineering & Agentic Topologies
title: Loop Engineering: Why Single-Turn Prompts Die and How Evaluator-Optimizer Loops Prevail
lead: Most engineers build agents as simple while-loops calling tools until the model stops. That is not agent architecture—that is an accident waiting for an infinite bill. Here is how modern Loop Engineering controls state, convergence, and evaluation.

stats.title: The True Cost of Naive Agent Loops:
items: In unconstrained ReAct loops, context length grows quadratically (O(N²)) with every tool step, meaning step 10 can cost 15x more tokens than step 1.
Production benchmarks show that switching from unguided ReAct to a Router-Worker + Evaluator-Optimizer topology boosts complex task completion from 47% to 91% while cutting total token spend in half.

mentalModel.title: 1. The 60-Second Mental Model: The Compiler Optimizer Pass
mentalModel.text:
When gcc or clang compiles your C++ code, it doesn't just read line 1 and emit machine code. It runs multiple discrete passes: lexing, AST construction, intermediate representation (IR), dead code elimination, and register allocation.

Loop Engineering treats LLM inference like an optimizing compiler pass. Rather than asking one monolithic prompt to 'Plan, Execute, Verify, and Format', we decouple the Planner, Worker, and Evaluator into distinct feedback circuits.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

MAX_EVAL_PASSES = 3
current_code = INITIAL_DRAFT_CODE

for iteration in range(MAX_EVAL_PASSES):
 # 1. EVALUATOR PASS: Claude acts strictly as an adversarial critic
 eval_response = client.messages.create(
 model="claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219",
 max_tokens=2048,
 system="You are an unforgiving static security auditor. Output <pass>true</pass> or <critique>reasons</critique>.",
 messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Audit this implementation:\n{current_code}"}]
 )
 eval_text = eval_response.content[0].text
 
 if "<pass>true</pass>" in eval_text:
 print(f" Converged successfully on iteration {iteration + 1}!")
 break
 
 # 2. OPTIMIZER PASS: Worker refactors based ONLY on the focused critique
 worker_response = client.messages.create(
 model="claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219",
 max_tokens=4096,
 system="Refactor the code to eliminate the auditor's specific security critiques.",
 messages=[
 {"role": "user", "content": f"Code:\n{current_code}\n\nCritique:\n{eval_text}"}
 ]
 )
 current_code = worker_response.content[0].text
else:
 print("️ Failed to reach convergence threshold. Halting.")

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: Never use the same prompt context for generation and self-evaluation; models suffer from confirmation bias on their own output.
Separate your agents: The Worker writes code, the Evaluator runs tests and critiques, and context is compacted between turns.
Enforce strict convergence criteria: max iterations, confidence threshold, and token budget.
takeaway.badge: Decoupling execution from evaluation prevents confirmation bias and stops hallucination loops.

import torch
from typing import Dict

def compute_task_vector(fine_weights: Dict[str, torch.Tensor], base_weights: Dict[str, torch.Tensor]) -> Dict[str, torch.Tensor]:
 """Calculate directional task vector: tau = W_fine - W_base."""
 return {k: fine_weights[k] - base_weights[k] for k in base_weights}

def ties_merge_task_vectors(task_vectors: list[Dict[str, torch.Tensor]], trim_fraction: float = 0.8) -> Dict[str, torch.Tensor]:
 """TIES-Merging: Trim noise, Elect consensus sign, Average aligned parameters."""
 merged_delta = {}
 for k in task_vectors[0].keys():
 deltas = torch.stack([tv[k] for tv in task_vectors]) # Shape: [N, ...]
 # 1. Trim redundant noise (keep top 20% magnitude deltas)
 flat = deltas.abs().flatten(start_dim=1)
 thresh = torch.quantile(flat, trim_fraction, dim=1, keepdim=True).unsqueeze(-1)
 mask = deltas.abs() >= thresh.view(deltas.shape[0], *([1] * (deltas.dim() - 1)))
 trimmed = deltas * mask
 # 2. Elect sign consensus
 sign_consensus = torch.sign(trimmed.sum(dim=0))
 # 3. Disjoint average aligned parameters
 aligned_mask = (torch.sign(trimmed) == sign_consensus) & mask
 counts = aligned_mask.sum(dim=0).clamp(min=1)
 merged_delta[k] = (trimmed * aligned_mask).sum(dim=0) / counts
 return merged_delta

def compose_deployment_checkpoint(base_weights: Dict[str, torch.Tensor], task_delta: Dict[str, torch.Tensor], scale: float = 0.5):
 return {k: base_weights[k] + scale * task_delta[k] for k in base_weights}

import json
import redis

r = redis.Redis(host="localhost", port=6379)

def execute_tool_idempotent(session_id: str, tool_name: str, arguments: dict, execute_fn):
 canonical_args = json.dumps(arguments, sort_keys=True)

 result = execute_fn(tool_name, arguments)
 r.setex(f"idemp:{idempotency_key}", 86400, json.dumps(result))
 return result
